title: Word Frequency Without a Null Pointer Exception
statement:
`Map<String, Integer>.get(key)` returns `null` for a key that is not
present -- not `0`, not an exception, `null`. That is a perfectly ordinary
reference-type return value right up until something tries to use it as a
number: `Integer` auto-unboxes to `int` wherever an `int` is expected, and
unboxing `null` has no sensible number to produce, so it throws instead.

## Your function

```
public static Map<String, Integer> wordFrequency(String text);
```

Return a map from each distinct whitespace-separated word in `text` to how
many times it occurs. `text` may be empty, in which case the result is an
empty map. Matching is case-sensitive: `"Cat"` and `"cat"` are different
words.

## Watch out

- **`counts.put(word, counts.get(word) + 1);` throws
  `NullPointerException` the first time `word` is seen.** `counts.get(word)`
  returns `null` for a word with no entry yet; `null + 1` has to unbox that
  `null` to a primitive `int` to perform the addition, and unboxing `null`
  is exactly what throws. This is legal, unremarkable-looking code --
  nothing about it warns you at compile time.
- **`counts.getOrDefault(word, 0)` returns `0` for a missing key instead
  of `null`** -- the identity element for "add one to the count", which
  is what makes `counts.put(word, counts.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1);`
  correct for a word's first occurrence and every later one, with the same
  line handling both.
- **`Map<String, Integer>.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)` does the same job
  in one call**, if you would rather reach for it: insert `1` if `word`
  is new, otherwise combine the existing value and `1` with the given
  function. Either `getOrDefault` or `merge` avoids the exception; a
  version that calls plain `get` and hopes for the best does not.
